e.t: This LXX Greek noun means “joy” or “rejoicing”—a glad response or state of delight. It names joyful celebration rather than an action word, and it can describe the happiness expressed in worship, deliverance, or festivity. The word occurs 19 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, with especially frequent use in Isaiah and Sirach. Its normal sense remains the positive experience or expression of gladness; the surrounding verse determines what brings about that joy.

This adjective means “adamantine,” describing something associated with adamant and characterized by exceptional hardness or firmness. It is a rare word in the Greek LXX corpus, occurring twice: once in Amos and once in 4 Maccabees. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise descriptive force in each passage cannot be stated more narrowly, but its central idea is hardness, strength, and resistance to yielding.

Azōtisti is a proper name referring to Azotisti. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 13:24. The lexical wording identifies the term as Azōtisti or Azotisti, but no broader definition or verse text is available here to explain its precise role in that occurrence. It belongs to the Greek LXX vocabulary and should remain distinct from Greek New Testament word entities.

This adjective describes something that sucks blood or is greedily hungry for blood. It portrays blood-seeking behavior in a sharply negative way, emphasizing an intense and destructive appetite rather than ordinary hunger. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, in 4 Maccabees 10:17. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its central meaning remains a blood-sucking or blood-greedy quality.

This Greek LXX noun means “pain,” referring to physical or inward suffering. It names the distress a person experiences rather than an action or command. The word appears six times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including three occurrences in Lamentations, where pain is especially prominent as a human experience. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains the experience of pain or anguish.

This noun means a rider—a person who rides, especially one mounted on an animal. In the Greek Old Testament, it commonly identifies mounted people rather than the animal itself. The word occurs 24 times across 20 verses, including passages in Exodus, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Haggai, and Zechariah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary meaning remains a mounted rider or group of riders.

This noun means “filling up”—the act or condition of being made full or complete. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Daniel, so its meaning is focused rather than broadly illustrated across many books. The word appears in Daniel 9:2 and Daniel 12:13, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its specific force in each passage. Its central idea remains the completion or fullness of something that has been lacking or unfinished.

This Greek LXX verb means “unfold” or “unroll”—to open something that has been folded or rolled so it lies open. It describes an action rather than an object, and its exact force depends on what is being opened in the surrounding verse. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, including uses in Deuteronomy, Judges, 2 Kings, and Ezekiel. Its clearest English rendering here is “unfold,” while “unroll” expresses the same basic action.

This verb means “resist”: to stand against something rather than accept or yield to it. It expresses opposition or refusal in action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Deuteronomy and once in Joshua. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the central idea remains active resistance or standing firm against an opposing force.

“Waterless” describes a place, condition, or thing that lacks water. As an adjective in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it points to dryness or the absence of a water supply rather than naming water itself. The word occurs 23 times in this corpus, with most occurrences in the Old Testament portion of the Greek Scriptures. Its broad use includes descriptions of dry settings and conditions where water is unavailable. The surrounding verse determines whether the word describes a landscape, a person’s situation, or another water-deprived condition.

This noun refers to concealment or a covering—something that hides or shields another thing from view. Its central idea is the act or condition of being covered rather than an action word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Job and Jeremiah, so it is relatively uncommon. One English rendering is “covering,” which fits its basic sense. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context.

This Greek LXX verb means “become petrified”—to become hard or stone-like. It describes a change of condition rather than simply naming a thing. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Exodus 15:16, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the sentence uses the verb.

Arbok, also rendered “Arvok,” is a proper name in the Greek Septuagint. It functions as a name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs five times in the Septuagint’s Old Testament, once in Genesis and four times in Joshua. Its appearances are concentrated in passages connected with the patriarchal and Israelite settlement narratives, but the available lexical information identifies the name without supplying a further definition or meaning beyond “Arbok” and “Arvok.”

Arour, also rendered Arur, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an idea or action. In the Greek Septuagint, it appears twice, once in Ezra 2:51 and once in Nehemiah 7:53. The available wording identifies the name but does not explain whether it refers to a particular person, family, or place. Its precise reference therefore depends on the surrounding lists and passages in those chapters.

This word means “infirmity” or “ailment,” referring to a condition of weakness or sickness. As a noun, it names the condition itself rather than the person who experiences it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times, including passages from Job, Psalms, Ecclesiastes, Jeremiah, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains a bodily or personal weakness understood as an ailment or infirmity.

Baani is a personal name, also represented as Vaani. It identifies an individual rather than describing an object, action, quality, or spiritual idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 8:10. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s particular role in that passage cannot be described further. Its basic meaning is therefore its use as a person’s name in that one recorded occurrence.

Baiōn, also rendered Veon, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. It identifies a particular named entity in the Greek Septuagint tradition, so its significance comes from what is being named in each passage, not from an abstract idea built into the word itself. It occurs three times in the LXX corpus: twice in Joshua and once in 1 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines the specific referent.

This noun means a “breach”—a break, opening, or damaged place in something that should be whole or secure. It can describe a physical gap needing repair, especially in a wall or structure. In this Greek Old Testament usage, the word appears nine times, all in 2 Kings, where it is associated with breaches requiring attention and repair. Its exact force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a damaged opening or break.

This word is a proper name, preserved in English as “Bēthanathinim” or “Vithanathinim.” It does not describe an action, quality, or ordinary object; it identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition. It occurs once, in Nehemiah 3:31. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its particular referent cannot be explained further here, but its lexical function is that of a name rather than a general description.

This Greek LXX verb means “slow”: to delay, move slowly, or take longer than expected. It describes slowness as an action or process rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it appears four times, spread across Genesis, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what or who is being described as slow, but the central idea remains delayed or unhurried action.

Gothoniel is a personal name, rendered as “Gothoniēl” or “Gothonil.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs eight times across seven verses, appearing in Joshua, Judges, and 1 Chronicles. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and account, but the word itself functions as a proper name for a person.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Delphōn; Thelfon.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Esther 9:7. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text or a description of the person or place involved, its exact referent must be understood from that passage. The name itself should therefore be retained as a proper name rather than expanded into a broader meaning.

This noun means “loosing one from another; separating.” It refers to the act or result of things or people being parted rather than held together. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it appears twice, once in Nehemiah and once in Sirach, so it is uncommon in these texts. Its basic idea is separation: a breaking apart or division between parties. The surrounding verse determines whether the word points to the act of separating or the condition produced by it.

Diospolis, also rendered Thiospolis, is a proper name for a place. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs twice, both times in Ezekiel: 30:14 and 30:16. The name itself identifies the location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. Its exact significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical function is simply to name Diospolis.

This adjective means “two-edged,” describing something made sharp or effective on both sides. It is used of an object or image whose two edges can cut, rather than of a one-sided blade. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, including passages in Judges, Psalms, Proverbs, and Sirach. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the noun or image it describes.

This adjective describes something that is hard to escape or inescapable. It can characterize a situation, condition, or thing from which escape is difficult or impossible. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 17:16, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. Its central sense remains clear: what cannot easily be escaped. The exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

Eder, also given as Ether, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a designation rather than a general description or action word. This name occurs two times in the LXX, both in 1 Chronicles: 23:23 and 24:30. The available wording preserves the name itself, but without the surrounding verse text, it does not establish whether the named individual or group is being identified in either passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “vindicate” or “avenge.” It describes acting to uphold a person’s claim or to answer a wrong with deserved judgment. The word can therefore refer either to defending someone whose cause needs to be established or to taking retribution against wrongdoing. It occurs 66 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its precise force depends on whether the surrounding passage emphasizes vindication or vengeance.

This verb means “sweep away,” describing the act of removing or carrying something off. It presents movement that clears something from its place rather than merely touching or moving it slightly. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Judges 5:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on sweeping something away or making it disappear from where it stood.

Eliasou, also rendered Eliasu, is a proper name referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 23:32. Because this word is a personal name and no further lexical definition is given, its central meaning is simply the individual’s name. Its precise significance in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage and the person being named.

This verb means “walk around in”: it describes moving about within a place or setting. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs seven times, so its basic sense is consistent, while its precise force depends on the sentence and surrounding passage. It can describe ordinary movement from place to place rather than merely arriving somewhere. The word appears in passages from Leviticus, Deuteronomy, 2 Samuel, Job, Proverbs, and Wisdom.

This verb means to impress something in—to make a mark, seal, or design pressed into another surface. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 15:4. The brief wording available does not establish the specific object being marked, but the central idea is a lasting impression made by pressing one thing into another.

This word means “inside,” referring to something located within an interior place or boundary. It can function as an adverb, describing where something is, or as a preposition, introducing what something is inside. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times across seven verses. Its uses span Psalms, Isaiah, Song of Songs, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees, so its basic sense remains a straightforward expression of inward location rather than an idea limited to one book or setting.

This verb means “conceal”: to hide something from view or keep it from being openly seen. It describes an action, so it focuses on what someone does to prevent something from being visible or exposed. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 19 times, showing that concealment is its consistent central sense across different passages. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being concealed and the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “manifest”: to make something known, clear, or visible. It describes something being brought into view or made plainly recognizable. The word occurs 29 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings represented here, so its basic sense is used across a range of passages rather than belonging to only one setting. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding text.

This verb expresses love, including being filled with passion. It describes strong personal affection rather than a merely neutral attitude, and it functions as an action word in the Greek Old Testament. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Esther 2:17 and Proverbs 4:6. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central sense remains passionate love directed toward a person or valued object.

This noun means “good order” or “order”—a condition in which things are arranged properly and function in an orderly way. It can describe organized conduct, a well-ordered situation, or the stability that comes from proper arrangement. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs four times, all in 4 Maccabees. The precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains order rather than confusion or disorder.

This Greek LXX noun means “thanks”—an expression of gratitude or thankful acknowledgment. It refers to giving thanks rather than to a person, object, or action by itself. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, including Esther, Wisdom, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains straightforward: recognizing a benefit, kindness, or favor with gratitude. The surrounding verse determines who gives thanks and what prompts it.

Zacharias is a proper name used for people in the Greek Old Testament and related Jewish writings. It identifies individuals rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears 46 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including books such as 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. Because several different people bear this name, the surrounding passage is needed to determine which Zacharias is meant in any particular verse. The English rendering is ordinarily “Zacharias.”

This adjective means “female” or “of women.” It identifies someone or something as belonging to the female sex and functions as a describing word rather than a name or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Numbers and once in Deuteronomy. Its basic meaning remains direct: it marks a person or creature as female. The surrounding verse determines what is being described, but the word itself supplies the female designation.

Tholmi is a proper name, preserved in English as “Tholmi.” It identifies a named figure or designation in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua, Judges, and 2 Samuel. Its exact reference is Joshua 15:14, Judges 1:10, and 2 Samuel 3:3; understanding the person or designation involved requires the surrounding verse and passage.

Iazēl, also rendered “Iazil,” is a proper name rather than a descriptive word. It identifies a named person, place, or other specific referent in the Greek Old Testament, though the available information does not establish which kind. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Joshua 19:18. Its precise referent must therefore be understood from that passage’s surrounding text.

This noun refers to the profaning or robbing of what belongs to a temple: “temple-robbery; sacrilege.” It describes an offense against a sacred place or its holy things, rather than ordinary theft. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 13:6. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains an act of treating sacred property or worship as something to violate or seize.

Irameel, also rendered Iramil, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament tradition and appears once, in 1 Chronicles 2:9. Because the name is preserved as a personal designation, its meaning here is the individual it names, not an expanded concept or description. The supplied material does not provide a separate definition or explanation of the name’s underlying sense.

This word is the proper name “Iōb; Iov,” referring to Job. It functions as a personal name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 63 times across 54 verses, appearing mainly in the book of Job and also twice in Ezekiel. Its repeated use identifies the same named figure wherever it occurs; the surrounding verse is needed to explain what is being said about him in a particular passage.

Kadmiel is a personal name, also rendered Kathmil. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs eight times, in Ezra and Nehemiah, including lists of returned families and accounts of worship and service. Because it is a name, its basic meaning is the person designated by it; the surrounding passage is needed to identify that person’s particular role in each occurrence.

This word means “beauty,” referring to the quality of being beautiful or pleasing to behold. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings to speak of beauty as a recognizable quality. The word occurs seven times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages in Psalms, Wisdom, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and subject.

This verb means to plaster over with something, describing the act of covering a surface by spreading plaster across it. It presents a practical action rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, showing a specific and uncommon word for applying a covering material. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic sense remains the act of coating or covering something with plaster.

Kaphira is a proper name, rendered “Kaphira” or “Kafira.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, once in Ezra 2:25 and once in Nehemiah 7:29. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its precise identity and role must be determined from those passages. The name itself carries no further lexical definition here.

This word means “harp,” a stringed musical instrument. As a noun, it names the instrument itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 24 times, with many occurrences in Psalms and several in Isaiah and Job, showing its regular place in descriptions of musical expression and accompaniment. Its earliest listed occurrence is Genesis 4:21, and its latest is 1 Maccabees 4:54. The precise significance of the harp in any verse depends on that passage’s surrounding words.

This word means “hollow,” describing an empty or concave space. It is a noun, so it refers to the hollow itself rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Psalms and Daniel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains a hollow or empty interior.

This noun means “cormorant,” the name of a bird. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Leviticus 11:16 and once in Deuteronomy 14:15. These are its only recorded occurrences in this corpus. The word identifies the bird itself, while the precise force of its use in either passage depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

This verb describes being extremely hungry or famished, expressing a strong bodily need for food. It refers to a person who lacks nourishment and feels hunger intensely. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Psalms, so its basic meaning is clear even though it is not common in this corpus. The English rendering “hungry” reflects this sense. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Makalōth, also written Makaloth, is a proper name. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in 1 Chronicles 8:31–32. The name itself does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it identifies someone or something named Makaloth. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent cannot be stated more specifically. The spelling Makalōth reflects a transliteration of the name rather than an English translation.

Masalami is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is therefore tied to the named individual or entity identified by the surrounding passage, not to a general concept that can be defined in ordinary terms. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 9:21. The available word information does not identify more about the name’s referent or explain its role in that verse.

Mattathias is a personal name, not a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it identifies people named Mattathias. The name occurs 21 times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, including seven occurrences in Old Testament books and fourteen in deuterocanonical books. It appears especially often in 1 Maccabees, but the name is also found in 1 Chronicles, Nehemiah, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise reference depends on the person and passage where the name occurs.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “stay; stand fast.” It describes remaining in place or continuing firmly rather than leaving or giving way. As a verb, it expresses an action or ongoing state of remaining. The word occurs 68 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including the deuterocanonical books, so it can serve in a range of settings while retaining this central sense. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means to “bear malice”—to hold resentment or ill will against someone rather than let an offense go. It describes an inward attitude of remembered hostility, not merely a passing feeling of displeasure. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times across five verses, showing a recurring concern with how people retain or express hostility toward others. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “ointment” or “perfume”—a fragrant substance used on the body, for preparation, or in worship. It can refer to a valuable scented mixture rather than an ordinary oil. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages about sacred preparation, burial customs, worship, feasting, and pleasant fragrance. Its exact significance in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Namna is a proper name, referring to a person named Namna rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 1:39. Because the available wording identifies only the name and does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, its normal meaning is simply the personal designation Namna. The surrounding genealogy supplies the specific identification of the person in that passage.

Nauath, also rendered Navath, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears six times, all within 1 Samuel 19–20. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide its meaning as a translated concept, it is best understood simply as the personal or place-name preserved in those passages. Its exact reference in each verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means to enlist strangers or levy mercenaries for service. It describes the act of gathering people from outside one’s own group, especially for military purposes. In its three recorded occurrences in the Greek LXX corpus, it appears in 1 Maccabees, so its use is limited but consistent with recruiting outsiders. The word focuses on the action of obtaining such people, rather than simply describing them as foreigners or strangers.

This adjective means “intact”: whole, complete, and not damaged or lacking a part. It describes something remaining in an undivided condition. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs nine times, so its basic idea is consistent while the surrounding noun determines what is whole or complete. The word appears in passages from Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Ezekiel, Zechariah, and other books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the person, object, or situation it describes.

Opheri, also rendered Oferi, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Numbers 26:36. The name identifies a particular person or family within that genealogical record, though the name itself does not provide a broader definition or explain the person’s character. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and genealogy.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “make a spectacle”: to expose someone or something publicly so it becomes an object of attention, often with shame or humiliation involved. It describes an action rather than a person or thing. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, each in a different verse, showing that its central idea is public display or exposure. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation.

This noun means “wanderer,” referring to a person who moves from place to place rather than remaining settled in one location. It is a descriptive term for such a person, and its precise force in a sentence depends on the surrounding passage. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Genesis 14:13. The available lexical sense is therefore clear, while the single occurrence does not establish a broader range of uses across different books or contexts.

Persea is a proper name, identifying something called “Persea” rather than describing an ordinary action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 8:5. The available information establishes the name and its grammatical function, but the verse text is not included, so the specific person, place, or thing it identifies cannot be determined from this word entry alone.

gl: of many years; full of years
d: of many years; full of years

e.t: This adjective describes someone or something connected with many years—being “of many years” or “full of years.” It points to extended age or duration rather than a brief period. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 4:16. The precise force of the adjective in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wording, but its central meaning is extended length of years.

Flight means the act or experience of fleeing or moving away. Its central idea is departure from a place or situation. In this LXX word, it functions as a noun, naming flight rather than describing an action as a verb. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at Jeremiah 28:39. The exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This verb means “prove before,” referring to establishing or demonstrating something in advance. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 2:25. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the prior demonstration or proof of something.

This LXX verb means “lie forth” or “lie before.” It describes something positioned out in front or set before someone, emphasizing its location or availability rather than an action of movement. The word appears 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, including Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Esther, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is said to be lying forth or before, but its central idea remains something placed openly in front.

This adjective describes something that is “giving forth fire.” It points to an object or thing characterized by producing or sending out fire, rather than simply possessing fire. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs only once, in 1 Maccabees 6:51. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided, the word’s precise reference there cannot be explained further; its basic meaning remains a description of something fire-emitting or fire-producing.

This Greek Old Testament verb means to “sprinkle” or “besprinkle”—to scatter or apply a small amount of liquid over something. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. The word appears 13 times in the Greek Old Testament, especially in Leviticus, where its use is associated with applying liquid in prescribed ritual actions. It also occurs in Exodus, Numbers, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on what is being sprinkled and the surrounding passage.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Sabathai” or “Savathe.” It identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 10:15. Because a personal name identifies someone instead of describing what the person is doing, its precise significance depends on the surrounding passage and the person’s role there.

Samia is a personal name, used to identify someone rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 9:16. Since no verse text or surrounding passage is available here, the name’s specific role in that verse cannot be described further. Its basic meaning is therefore the proper name “Samia,” functioning as a person’s designation in the text.

Sarabia is a proper name, also rendered Saravia. It identifies someone or something named Sarabia in the Greek Old Testament text. The name occurs five times, all in Nehemiah, from Nehemiah 8:7 through Nehemiah 12:24. Because the available information does not include the surrounding verse text, it does not establish whether each occurrence refers to a person, a family, or another named entity. Its precise reference therefore depends on the passage where it appears.

Saphōn, also rendered Safon, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs twice in the Greek LXX: once in Genesis 46:16 and once in Numbers 26:24. Without the surrounding verse text, its personal identity and significance in each passage cannot be explained further here.

This word is a proper name referring to a place called Sēn, also rendered Sin. It functions as a geographical name rather than a description of a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 20 times across 19 verses. Its uses span books such as Joshua, Proverbs, Isaiah, Wisdom, and 3 Maccabees, showing that it remains a place-name wherever it appears. The surrounding verse is needed to identify the specific location or role intended in each passage.

This noun means “carpenter’s axe” or “axe,” referring to a tool used for cutting or shaping wood. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 1 Chronicles 20:3. The word therefore names an ordinary implement rather than an action, person, or quality. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a carpenter’s axe or axe.

This Greek LXX noun means “Booths,” referring to shelters or structures identified by that name. It occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings represented here, including passages in Deuteronomy, Zechariah, 1 Maccabees, and 2 Maccabees. The word itself names the booths rather than describing an action or attitude. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

This verb means “stain”: to mark something with an unwanted blemish or make it impure. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its exact force depends on what is being stained in the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Wisdom 15:4. The word’s central idea remains the same whether the stain is understood physically or figuratively: something clean or acceptable is marked by an undesirable impurity.

gl: one who collects and writes down historic facts; historian
d: one who collects and writes down historic facts; historian

e.t: This Greek noun means “one who collects and writes down historic facts; historian.” It describes a person who gathers information and records historical matters in writing. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 2:28. Its basic emphasis is on careful collection and written preservation of historical facts, rather than on a general speaker or storyteller. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the particular role the person has in that passage.

This Greek LXX adverb means “vehemently” or “tremendously,” expressing a very strong degree or intensity. It describes how strongly something happens, how great something is, or how deeply someone responds. Thus, it can intensify an action, condition, or description rather than name a person or thing. The word occurs 362 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its exact force is shaped by the sentence in which it appears. Its central idea remains strong intensity or exceptional measure.

This word refers to a mastich-tree, a tree associated with producing mastich resin. It is a noun, naming the tree itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Susanna 1:54. The word’s basic meaning is therefore specific and concrete: it identifies a particular kind of tree. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the lexical sense remains “mastich-tree.”

This verb means “turn,” describing a change in direction or movement. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua 11:6. The basic sense is an action of turning rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the precise force of the word in that occurrence must be understood from its immediate context. Its lexical meaning remains a straightforward expression of turning.

This word means “you,” referring to the people being addressed. It is a pronoun, so it points to its hearers or readers rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it appears 651 times, showing that it is a common way of directly addressing others. Its use ranges across many biblical books, including Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. The surrounding words determine exactly whom it addresses in each passage.

This LXX verb means “overlook”: to pass over something without acting on it or giving it the usual attention. It describes an action rather than a person or object, and its precise force depends on what is being overlooked in the sentence. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus, including three occurrences in Leviticus. Its basic idea remains the same wherever it appears: something is seen or considered, yet not dealt with in the expected way.

This noun means a supposition or consideration—a thought formed by reflecting on something or taking it into account. It describes an idea or judgment held in the mind, rather than an action itself. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 25:7. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central sense remains an assumption or mental consideration.

“Phangai” or “Fangge” is a proper name for a place. It is not presented as an ordinary description or action word, but as the name of a specific location in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Joshua 19:12. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself identifies the place but does not establish additional meaning, symbolism, or significance. Its precise role in that passage depends on the geographic and textual context of Joshua 19.

Phardatha, also rendered Farthatha, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament text. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Esther 9:8. The available wording identifies the name itself, but without the verse text this entry cannot explain the person’s role or significance in that passage.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a person’s “feeling” or “wits”—the inward capacity by which someone senses, understands, or thinks. It can therefore describe a person’s inner awareness or sound judgment rather than an outward action. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, including eight occurrences in Proverbs. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on how the surrounding sentence uses this idea.

Chaphenatha, also rendered Khafenatha, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or place in the Greek LXX-related corpus, but the available lexical information does not specify which. This name occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 12:37. Its precise referent and significance must therefore be determined from the surrounding passage rather than from the name itself.

Chettiim, also rendered Khettim, is a proper name used to identify a named people or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition. Its meaning is not an ordinary action, quality, or object; it functions as a designation. This LXX word occurs twice in the supplied corpus, once in Jeremiah and once in 1 Maccabees. The form “Chettiim” is preserved in the English rendering of 1 Maccabees 1:1, while the lexical definition gives both “Chettiim” and “Khettim” as approved renderings of the name.

This Greek LXX noun means “capital,” referring to the uppermost or crowning part of something, especially the top of a column or similar structure. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament text, all within 2 Kings 25:17. The word identifies a physical architectural feature rather than expressing an action, quality, or personal title. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding description, but its central meaning remains the crowning top or upper part of a structure.

This word means “barring; apart from.” It marks something as excluded, separated, or left outside what is being discussed. As an adverb or preposition, it can show that a person or thing is considered separately from others, or that a condition does not include it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 14 times, across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is separation or exclusion.

This verb means to “make an inarticulate noise; sound.” It describes producing a noise rather than expressing clear words or a developed statement. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 6:11. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the exact force of the sound in that passage cannot be specified beyond this basic meaning. The word’s central idea is audible noise or sound made by someone or something.
